The modern esports boom has also seen a rise in video games companies embracing the esports potential of their products. After many years of ignoring and at times suppressing the esports scene, Nintendo hosted Wii Games Summer 2010. Spanning over a month, the tournament had over 400,000 participants, making it the largest and most expansive tournament in the company's history. In 2014 Nintendo hosted an invitational Super Smash Bros. for Wii U competitive tournament at the 2014 Electronic Entertainment Expo (E3) press conference that was streamed online on Twitch.[60] Halo developers 343 Industries announced in 2014 plans to revive Halo as an esport with the creation of the Halo Championship Series and a prize pool of US$50,000.[61] Both Blizzard Entertainment and Riot Games have their own collegiate outreach programs with their North American Collegiate Championship.[62][63] Since 2013 universities and colleges in the United States such as Robert Morris University Illinois and the University of Pikeville have recognized esports players as varsity level athletes and offer athletic scholarships.[64] In 2017, Tespa, Blizzard Entertainment's collegiate esports division, unveiled its new initiative to provide scholarships and prizes for collegiate esports clubs competing in its tournaments worth US$1 million.[65] Colleges have begun granting scholarships to students who qualify to play esports professionally for the school. Colleges such as Columbia College, Robert Morris University, and Indiana Institute of Technology have taken part in this.[66] In 2018, Harrisburg University of Science and Technology began a tuition scholarship program for esports players.[67]
Esports commentator Froskurinn in 2017
In 2014, the largest independent esports league, Electronic Sports League, partnered with the local brand Japan Competitive Gaming to try and grow esports in the country.[68]
Physical viewership of esports competitions and the scope of events have increased in tandem with the growth of online viewership.[69] In 2013, the Season 3 League of Legends World Championship was held in a sold-out Staples Center.[70] The 2014 League of Legends World Championship in Seoul, South Korea, had over 40,000 fans in attendance and featured the band Imagine Dragons, and opening and closing ceremonies in addition to the competition.[71]

In 2015, the first Esports Arena was launched in Santa Ana, California, as the United States' first dedicated esports facility.[72]
The global esports audience reached 662.6 million in 2020, and 921 million in 2022.[73]
In 2021, China announced a law which forbade minors from playing video games – which they described as "spiritual opium" – for more than three hours a week.[74] With China being a large market, the law raised concerns about the future of esports within the country.[75][76][77]
Classification as a sport  
A match of Tekken 7 at the 2019 Southeast Asian Games. Esports was a medal event at the regional games which featured mostly traditional sports.
Labeling competitive video games as a sport is a controversial topic.[78][79] Proponents[80] argue that esports are a fast-growing "non-traditional sport" which requires "careful planning, precise timing, and skillful execution".[81] Others claim that sports involve physical fitness and physical training, and prefer to classify esports as a mind sport.[82]
Former ESPN president John Skipper described esports in 2014 as a competition and "not a sport".[83][84][85][86][87][88] In 2013 on an episode of Real Sports with Bryant Gumbel the panelist openly laughed at the topic.[89] In addition, many in the fighting games community maintain a distinction between their competitive gaming competitions and the more commercially connected esports competitions of other genres.[90] In the 2015 World Championship hosted by the International Esports Federation, an esports panel of guests from international sports society discussed the future recognition of esports as a legitimate sport.[91]

Russia was the first country that classified "cybersport" as an official sport discipline[92] on 25 July 2001.[93] After a series of reforms in Russian sports, it was classified as a sport again on 12 March 2004.[93][94][95][96] In July 2006, it was removed from a list of sport disciplines because it did not fit the new sport standards.[97][98] On 7 July 2016, The Ministry of Sport decided to add cybersport into the sport registry[99] and on 13 April 2017, esports become an official sport discipline once again.[citation needed]
China was another one of the first countries to recognize esports as a real sport in 2003,[100] despite concerns at the time that video games were addictive. Through this, the government encouraged esports, stating that by participating in esports, players were also "training the body for China".[101] Furthermore, by early 2019, China recognized esports players as an official profession within the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security's Occupation Skill Testing Authority recommendations, as well as professional gaming operators, those that distribute and manage esports games.[102] By July 2019, more than 100,000 people had registered themselves as professional gamers under this, with the Ministry stating that they anticipate over 2 million such people in this profession in five years.[103]
In 2013, Canadian League of Legends player Danny "Shiphtur" Le became the first pro gamer to receive an American P-1A visa, a category designated for "Internationally Recognized Athletes".[104][105] In 2014, Turkey's Ministry of Youth and Sports started issuing esports licenses to players certified as professionals.[106][107] In 2016, the French government started working on a project to regulate and recognize esports.[108] The Games and Amusements Board of the Philippines started issuing athletic licenses to Filipino esports players who are vouched for by a professional esports team in July 2017.[109][110]

To help promote esports as a legitimate sport, several esports events have been run alongside more traditional international sports competitions. The 2007 Asian Indoor Games was the first notable multi-sport competition including esports as an official medal-winning event, alongside other traditional sports, and the later editions of the Asian Indoor Games, as well as its successor the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games, have always included esports as an official medal event or an exhibition event up to now. Moreover, the Asian Games, which is the Asian top-level multi-sport competition, also included esports as a medal event at the 2022 edition; esports around games such as Hearthstone, Starcraft II, and League of Legends were presented as an exhibition event at the 2018 Asian Games as a lead-in to the 2022 games.[111][112] The 2019 Southeast Asian Games included six medal events for esports.[113] Since 2018, World Sailing has held an eSailing World Championship that showed a main sports federation embracing esports.[114] The Virtual Regatta race shadowing the 2020-2021 Vendee Globe was the first online game believe to have in excess of 1,000,000 unique users[115]
Ahead of The International 2021, which was originally set to take place in Stockholm in 2020, the Swedish Sports Confederation voted in June 2021 to deny recognition of esports as a sporting event, which jeopardized plans for how Valve had arranged the event in regards to travel visas for international players. Valve had tried to work with Sweden to accommodate players, but eventually rescheduled the event to Romania instead.[116][117]
The 2022 Commonwealth Games featured esports competitions as a pilot ahead of being a potential full medal event for 2026.[118]
In Greece, in March 2022 a law entered into force recognising and regulating esports[119] and in June 2023, the relevant federation for esports has been officially given recognition[120] and included in the list of sports federations.[121]
Olympic Games recognition

The Olympic Games are also seen as a potential method to legitimize esports. A summit held by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) in October 2017 acknowledged the growing popularity of esports, concluding that "Competitive 'esports' could be considered as a sporting activity, and the players involved prepare and train with an intensity which may be comparable to athletes in traditional sports" but would require any games used for the Olympics fitting "with the rules and regulations of the Olympic movement".[122] Another article by Andy Stout suggests that 106 million people viewed the 2017 Worlds Esports competition.[123] International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Thomas Bach has noted that the IOC is troubled by violent games and the lack of a global sanctioning body for esports.[124][112] Bach acknowledged that many Olympic sports originated from violent combat, but stated that "sport is the civilized expression about this. If you have egames where it's about killing somebody, this cannot be brought into line with our Olympic values."[112] Due to that, the IOC suggested that they would approve more esports centered around games that simulate real sports, such as the NBA 2K or FIFA series.[125]

The issues around esports have not prevented the IOC from exploring what possibilities there are for incorporation into future Olympics. In July 2018, the IOC and the Global Association of International Sports Federations (GAISF) held a symposium and invited major figures in esports, including Epic Games' Mark Rein, Blizzard Entertainment's Mike Morhaime, and esports players Dario "TLO" Wünsch, Jacob "Jake" Lyon, and Se-yeon "Geguri" Kim, for these organizations "to gain a deeper understanding of esports, their impact and likely future development, so that [they] can jointly consider the ways in which [they] may collaborate to the mutual benefit of all of sport in the years ahead".[126][127] The IOC has tested the potential for esports through exhibition games. With support from the IOC, Intel sponsored exhibition esports events for StarCraft II and Steep prior to the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, and five South Korean esports players were part of the Olympic Torch relay.[128][129] A similar exhibition showcase, the eGames, was held alongside the 2016 Summer Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, though this was not supported by the IOC.
During the Eighth Olympic Summit in December 2019, the IOC reiterated that it would only consider sports-simulating games for any official Olympic event, but it would look at two paths for such games in the future: those that promoted good physical and mental health lifestyles, and virtual reality and augmented reality games that included physical activity.[130]

In the late 2010s, leaders in Japan became involved in helping bring esports to the 2020 Summer Olympics and beyond, given the country's reputation as a major video game industry centre. Esports in Japan had not flourished due to the country's anti-gambling laws that also prevent paid professional gaming tournaments, but there were efforts starting in late 2017 to eliminate this issue.[10] At the suggestion of the Tokyo Olympic Games Committee for the 2020 Summer Olympics, four esports organizations have worked with Japan's leading consumer organization to exempt esports tournaments from gambling law restrictions. Takeo Kawamura, a member of the Japanese House of Representatives and of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, led a coalition of ruling and opposing politicians to support esports, called the Japan esports Union, or JeSU.[131] Kawamura said that they would be willing to pass laws to further exempt esports as needed so that esports athletes can make a living playing these sports. So far, this has resulted in the ability of esports players to obtain exemption licenses to allow them to play, a similar mechanism needed for professional athletes in other sports in Japan to play professionally.[10] The first such licenses were given out in mid-July 2018, via a tournament held by several video game publishers to award prizes to many players but with JeSU offering these exemption licenses to the top dozen or so players that emerge, allowing them to compete in further esports events.[131] The Tokyo Olympic Committee has also planned to arrange a number of esports events leading up to the 2020 games.[10] With the IOC, five esports events were set as part of an Olympic Virtual Series from 13 May to 23 June 2021, ahead of the games. Each event in auto racing, baseball, cycling, rowing and sailing will be managed by an IOC-recognized governing body for the sport along with a video game publisher of a game for that sport. For example, the auto racing event will be based on the Gran Turismo series and overseen by the International Automobile Federation along with Polyphony Digital. The baseball, cycling, and esailing events will be based on eBaseball Powerful Pro Baseball 2020, Zwift, and Virtual Regatta, respectively.[132]

# Dennis Quaid, wife Kimberly divorcing ‘with mutual respect’
By Frank Lovece
…Comments
Posted on June 29, 2016
Actor Dennis Quaid and his third wife, Kimberly Buffington Quaid, have announced they are divorcing.
Video 3
Video 4
Skip Ad
“After careful consideration, we have decided to end our 12-year marriage,” the couple said in a statement Wednesday to TMZ.com. “The decision was made amicably and with mutual respect toward one another.”
The two had met in Austin, Texas, in March 2003, when a mutual friend introduced them at a dinner. They married on July 4, 2004, and had twins Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace on Nov. 8, 2007. Quaid, 62, also has a son, actor Jack Quaid, 24, with his second wife, Meg Ryan, to whom he was married from 1991 to 2001. He previously was wed to actress P.J. Soles from 1978 to 1983.
Buffington Quaid initially filed for divorce on March 2, 2012, citing irreconcilable differences, but the couple soon reunited. She then filed for legal separation on Oct. 19 of that year, with Dennis Quaid subsequently filing for divorce that Nov. 30. Though the actor’s representative the following March denied rumors that the couple had reconciled, telling E! News, “They are divorcing,” they withdrew the petition by that September.

# Dennis Quaid, wife Kimberly divorcing ‘with mutual respect’
By Frank Lovece
…Comments
Posted on June 29, 2016
Actor Dennis Quaid and his third wife, Kimberly Buffington Quaid, have announced they are divorcing.
Video 3
Video 4
Skip Ad
“After careful consideration, we have decided to end our 12-year marriage,” the couple said in a statement Wednesday to TMZ.com. “The decision was made amicably and with mutual respect toward one another.”
The two had met in Austin, Texas, in March 2003, when a mutual friend introduced them at a dinner. They married on July 4, 2004, and had twins Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace on Nov. 8, 2007. Quaid, 62, also has a son, actor Jack Quaid, 24, with his second wife, Meg Ryan, to whom he was married from 1991 to 2001. He previously was wed to actress P.J. Soles from 1978 to 1983.
Buffington Quaid initially filed for divorce on March 2, 2012, citing irreconcilable differences, but the couple soon reunited. She then filed for legal separation on Oct. 19 of that year, with Dennis Quaid subsequently filing for divorce that Nov. 30. Though the actor’s representative the following March denied rumors that the couple had reconciled, telling E! News, “They are divorcing,” they withdrew the petition by that September.

**Envy** (stylized in all caps as **ENVY**), formerly **Team Envy**, is an American esports franchise based in Dallas, Texas. Founded in 2007 as a professional _Call of Duty_ team under the moniker **Team EnVyUs**, they fielded rosters in _Counter-Strike, FIFA, Fortnite, Gears of War, Halo, League of Legends, Chess, Magic: the Gathering, Overwatch, Paladins, [PUBG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayerUnknown's\_Battlegrounds "PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds"), Rocket League, SMITE, StarCraft, [Super Smash Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros. "Super Smash Bros."), Street Fighter_ and _Valorant_ in their original form. Following the merger between Envy Gaming and OpTic Gaming, Envy Gaming retired the Team Envy brand in June 2022, shifting all of them to the OpTic Gaming moniker.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-2)
On January 17, 2025, Mike "Hastr0" Rufail announced that he had re-acquired the Team Envy name, as well as associated trademarks, from OpTic, reviving the franchise as ENVY.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-EnvyRevival-3) Envy has since entered _Apex Legends_, _Marvel Rivals_, _The Finals_ and _[Rainbow Six Siege X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom\_Clancy's\_Rainbow\_Six\_Siege "Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege")_, as well as re-entering _Counter-Strike_, _Halo_, _Super Smash Bros._ and Valorant (currently as members of the Valorant Champions Tour (VCT) Americas).
Owner and CEO Mike "Hastr0" Rufail played for the team's _Call of Duty_ team.

Team EnVyUs was founded on November 19, 2007, as a _Call of Duty 4_ esports team by Skyler "FoRePlayy" Johnson and Tosh "Stainville" McGruder. The team finished runners-up in both the 2008 and 2009MLG National Championships, with the 2009 roster fielding future owner Mike "Hastr0" Rufail.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:02-4)
At the 2011 National Championship, the final event of the Call of Duty: Black Ops season, Envy once again finished runners-up following a 5-match loser's bracket run; the event also marked the beginning of the classic rivalry with OpTic Gaming, dubbed the eClasico, after defeating them in the loser's bracket final.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-6)

In April 2013, as part of the _Call of Duty: Black Ops II_ season, Envy competed in the inaugural US$1 million Call of Duty Championship; their roster for the tournament notably included Stainville, Raymond "Rambo" Lussier and Jordan "JKap" Kaplan. Non-favorites entering the event, the team showed they belonged after beating the undefeated Fariko Impact 3–2 in the winner's bracket finals to book a place in the grand finals. The grand finals consisted of a best-of-11 continuation series re-match with Fariko, where Envy would fall just short after losing 5–6 following a game 11 Search and Destroy, winner-takes-all, showdown. The final round earned the title of "the most famous round of Search and Destroy in Call of Duty history", as well as the match being widely considered one of the "greatest series ever played" in _Call of Duty_ history.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:2-7) The following month, on May 5, Team Envy won their first ever prized LAN championship and only Black Ops II title at UGC Niagara.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-9)

In March 2014, as part of the _Call of Duty: Ghosts_ season, Envy competed in the 2014 Call of Duty Championship. The team would once again finish 2nd after producing a miracle run starting from round 1 of the loser's bracket, including a 3–1 victory over OpTic in the loser's bracket final.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:5-10) On June 25, 2014, they announced the return of JKap and the acquisition of Matthew "Formal" Piper.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-11) The new roster won Gfinity 3, Envy's first major LAN championship, and Season 3 of MLG's Ghosts Pro League. However, the roster was short-lived as after ESWC 2014, the last event of Ghosts, star AR player Formal and Envy mutually agreed to part ways.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-12)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)
Moving into _Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare_, Envy made multiple roster changes throughout a disappointing season. The team managed a top-12 finish at the 2015 Call of Duty Championship, before reaching their only final at UGC Niagara 2015. They ended the season with a 4th-place finish at the 2015 MLG World Finals.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)

In April 2016, Envy acquired Bryan "Apathy" Zhelyazkov and Johnathon "John" Perez to join JKap and Austin "SlasheR" Liddicoat for the latter half of the Call of Duty: Black Ops III season.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-14) Together they won Stage 2 of the NA Call of Duty World League, Envy's first major championship since Ghosts.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-15) The team then participated at the 2016 MLG Orlando Open, where following a loser's bracket run they met OpTic in the grand finals. In the finals they took the first best-of-5 series 3–2, before being swept in the deciding series.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8) In the last event of the season, in September 2016, Envy competed in the 2016 Call of Duty World League Championship. The team went undefeated in the group stages and drew a winner's bracket round 1 match-up with heavy favorites OpTic, who they had not defeated on LAN in over two years. A 3–1 victory over OpTic, followed by a 3–0 over FaZe Clan opened the path to the grand finals where they met Splyce in the first ever North American vs. European final. Team Envy took down Splyce 3–1 to finally break their 2nd place curse and win the Call of Duty Championship; securing $800,000 as part of the largest Call of Duty prize pool.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:6-16)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:4-17)

Maintaining their championship winning roster, they headed into the _Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare_season. The first three-quarters of the season proved disappointing as the team failed to live up to their Black Ops III success, with their only notable result being a 3rd-place finish at the 2017 MLG Atlanta Open in February 2017.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-18) It was not until the last two events that Envy bounced back. In July 2017, the team finished runners-up at Stage 2 of the 2017 CWL Global Pro League.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-19) In August 2017, they competed in the 2017 Call of Duty World League Championship where they attempted to become the first back-to-back champions. In the winner's bracket semi-finals they defeated eUnited 3–1, which included their famous second half 0–10 to 12–10 Uplink comeback.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-20) In the winner's bracket final they defeated OpTic to book their place in a record 4th Call of Duty Championship grand finals, however this time around the roster would be heartbroken as they lost both best-of-5 series to OpTic in a rematch to finish in 2nd place.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:7-21)
Heading into _Call of Duty: WWII_, Envy released JKap, Apathy, and John.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-22) In November 2017, they revealed their new roster which included Cuyler "Huke" Garland who had been competing in Team Envy's Halo division as he was too young (under the age of 18) to compete in the Call of Duty World League.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-23)

On September 22, 2018, Envy acquired the roster of Evil Geniuses consisting of ACHES, Apathy, Assault and SiLLy. They will join the organization and pair with Huke to complete the roster.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-24)
Team Envy's parent company Envy Gaming purchased a Call of Duty League slot in late 2019, ending Team Envy's _Call of Duty_ division. The team, Dallas Empire, competes in the league in the 2020 season.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-25)
Team Envy officially entered the _Counter-Strike_ scene, their first venture into PC Esports, on February 2, 2015, after acquiring the French _Counter-Strike: Global Offensive_ (_CS:GO_) squad of Team LDLC led by captain Vincent "Happy" Schopenhauer.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-26)

In March 2015, Envy finished 3rd–4th in their first major appearance, ESL One Katowice 2015, after losing to Ninjas in Pyjamas 0–2 in the semi-finals.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-27) Shortly afterwards, in March, the team won their first ever championship at the Gfinity Spring Masters.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-28) On June 21, 2015, they traded Richard "shox" Papillon and Edouard "SmithZz" Dubourdeaux to Titan in exchange for Kenny "kennyS" Schrub and Dan "apEX" Madesclaire.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-29) With the new roster they finished runners-up at the ESL One Cologne 2015 major, before finally winning their first major championship at DreamHack Open Cluj-Napoca 2015 after defeating Natus Vincere 2–0 in the grand finals.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:8-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:9-31) Following the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks, Envy withdrew from IEM San Jose due to travel safety concerns.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-32) The team ended the 2015 season securing 7 championships and 11 grand final appearances.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33)

In March 2016, following an 11–12th-place finish at IEM Katowice 2016, Envy benched Fabien "kioShiMa" Fiey due to communication problems and LDLC White's Timothée "DEVIL" Démolon replaced him in the starting line-up.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33) However, the change would prove unsuccessful and in October 2016, DEVIL was released with Christophe "SIXER" Xia replacing him.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-35) On January 15, 2017, the team won WESG 2016, securing US$800,000 as part of the largest CS:GO prize pool.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:10-36)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:4-17)
In February 2017, kennyS, apEX, and Nathan "NBK" Schmitt departed to G2 Esports, with Adil "ScreaM" Benrlitom, Cédric "RpK" Guipouy, and Alexandre "xms" Forté joining in their stead.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-38) In late April, Envy officially revealed their academy project.

On June 20, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the _Counter-Strike_ esports scene following the release of their entire CS:GO roster.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-40) On September 27, 2018, they announced a new North American team, signing the core of ex-Splyce.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:15-41) Team Envy disbanded their _CS:GO_ division on January 11, 2021.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-42)
On September 29, 2026, Envy would return to _Counter-Strike_ for their first _Counter-Strike 2_ roster, signing the 3DMAX roster following the French organization's financial troubles.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-43)

The Team Envy _Gears of War_ (_GoW_) division was founded on January 4, 2012, when the organization formed the professional _GoW_ team "EnVyUs MbN".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-44) The team competed in Gears of War 3, where they placed 4th in the LAN tournament Hypefestation 2.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-46)
In October 2015, Envy announced they were re-entering the _GoW_ competitive scene for Gears of War: Ultimate Edition and were revealed as one of eight teams in ESL's GoW Pro League.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-48) In Season 1 of the league, Envy finished runners-up to Denial Esports.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-49) In Season 2, they became champions after defeating Denial in a rematch of the finals following a 12–2 regular season record; the tournament win marked their first ever Gears of War title.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-50) In July 2016, without dropping a single map, Envy won their second title at the Gears eSports European Open in London.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-51)

Heading into _Gears of War 4_, Envy competed in the Coalition's $1 million Gears Pro Circuit.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-52) Their campaign included multiple second-place finishes, as well as the team's third championship in January 2017, when the team dethroned OpTic Gaming at the Mexico City Open, the first ever GoW event in Latin America.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-54)
On June 13, 2017, shortly after the end of the Gears Pro Circuit, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Gears of War esports scene following the transfer of their roster to Echo Fox.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-55)
The Team Envy _Halo_ division was founded on November 10, 2015, when the organization signed a professional esports team for _Halo 5: Guardians_; the roster included Justin "Pistola" Deese and Austin "Mickwen" McCleary.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-57) The team failed to qualify for the 2016 Halo World Championship after being knocked out of the group stages at the NA Regional Finals.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-58)

Their first major breakthrough came in July 2016, when the team finished 3rd place at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Summer Finals.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-59) In the offseason to follow, Envy acquired rookie Cuyler "Huke" Garland and veteran Eric "Snip3down" Wrona.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-60) In November, they obtained their first Halo championship after winning HCS Las Vegas 2016.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:12-61) Shortly afterwards, in December, the team dethroned OpTic Gaming and won their second championship at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Fall Finals.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-62) Their 2016–17 season campaign ended with a runners-up finish at the 2017 Halo World Championship, where the team produced a 5–0 loser's bracket run before losing to OpTic Gaming in the grand finals.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:13-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-64)
In May 2017, Envy won their third Halo championship at HCS Daytona 2017.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-65) Their 2017–18 season campaign ended in April 2018, following a 3rd-place finish at the 2018 Halo World Championship.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:14-66) On May 24, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Halo esports scene following the release of their roster.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-67)

Team Envy announced their return to the _Halo_ esports scene on October 12, 2020, announcing four new players to compete under head coach Alex "Swift Kill" Ramirez for the upcoming _Halo_ franchise game _Halo Infinite_.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-68) After the merger of Envy Gaming and OpTic Gaming in 2021, OpTic took over Team Envy's _Halo_ division.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-69)
On May 18, 2016, after passing Riot's vetting process, Team Envy officially purchased Renegades’ NA LCS spot in a deal reportedly valued in excess of $1 million.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:622-70)
In their inaugural split, following a perfect 4–0 start, Envy finished in 6th place achieving a playoffs berth, where they were eliminated in the first round.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-71) In the last chance Regional Qualifier for the 2016 League of Legends World Championship, the team once again fell short after losing in the second round to eventual winners Cloud9.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-72)
Following the 2017 Spring Split, Envy faced relegation and had to compete in the Summer Promotion Tournament. In the Promotion Tournament, they qualified into the 2017 NA LCS Summer Split after defeating Gold Coin United 3–2 in the loser's bracket finals.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-73)
On November 20, 2017, Team Envy withdrew from League of Legends after their franchise application for the 2018 NA LCS season was declined.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-75)

The team would once again finish 2nd after producing a miracle run starting from round 1 of the loser's bracket, including a 3–1 victory over OpTic in the loser's bracket final.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:5-10) On June 25, 2014, they announced the return of JKap and the acquisition of Matthew "Formal" Piper.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-11) The new roster won Gfinity 3, Envy's first major LAN championship, and Season 3 of MLG's Ghosts Pro League. However, the roster was short-lived as after ESWC 2014, the last event of Ghosts, star AR player Formal and Envy mutually agreed to part ways.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-12)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)
Moving into _Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare_, Envy made multiple roster changes throughout a disappointing season. The team managed a top-12 finish at the 2015 Call of Duty Championship, before reaching their only final at UGC Niagara 2015. They ended the season with a 4th-place finish at the 2015 MLG World Finals.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)
texts.5: In April 2016, Envy acquired Bryan "Apathy" Zhelyazkov and Johnathon "John" Perez to join JKap and Austin "SlasheR" Liddicoat for the latter half of the Call of Duty: Black Ops III season.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-14) Together they won Stage 2 of the NA Call of Duty World League, Envy's first major championship since Ghosts.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-15) The team then participated at the 2016 MLG Orlando Open, where following a loser's bracket run they met OpTic in the grand finals. In the finals they took the first best-of-5 series 3–2, before being swept in the deciding series.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8) In the last event of the season, in September 2016, Envy competed in the 2016 Call of Duty World League Championship. The team went undefeated in the group stages and drew a winner's bracket round 1 match-up with heavy favorites OpTic, who they had not defeated on LAN in over two years. A 3–1 victory over OpTic, followed by a 3–0 over FaZe Clan opened the path to the grand finals where they met Splyce in the first ever North American vs. European final. Team Envy took down Splyce 3–1 to finally break their 2nd place curse and win the Call of Duty Championship; securing $800,000 as part of the largest Call of Duty prize pool.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:6-16)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:3-8)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:4-17)
texts.6:
Maintaining their championship winning roster, they headed into the _Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare_season. The first three-quarters of the season proved disappointing as the team failed to live up to their Black Ops III success, with their only notable result being a 3rd-place finish at the 2017 MLG Atlanta Open in February 2017.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-18) It was not until the last two events that Envy bounced back. In July 2017, the team finished runners-up at Stage 2 of the 2017 CWL Global Pro League.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-19) In August 2017, they competed in the 2017 Call of Duty World League Championship where they attempted to become the first back-to-back champions. In the winner's bracket semi-finals they defeated eUnited 3–1, which included their famous second half 0–10 to 12–10 Uplink comeback.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-20) In the winner's bracket final they defeated OpTic to book their place in a record 4th Call of Duty Championship grand finals, however this time around the roster would be heartbroken as they lost both best-of-5 series to OpTic in a rematch to finish in 2nd place.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:7-21)
Heading into _Call of Duty: WWII_, Envy released JKap, Apathy, and John.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-22) In November 2017, they revealed their new roster which included Cuyler "Huke" Garland who had been competing in Team Envy's Halo division as he was too young (under the age of 18) to compete in the Call of Duty World League.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-23)
texts.7:
On September 22, 2018, Envy acquired the roster of Evil Geniuses consisting of ACHES, Apathy, Assault and SiLLy. They will join the organization and pair with Huke to complete the roster.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-24)
Team Envy's parent company Envy Gaming purchased a Call of Duty League slot in late 2019, ending Team Envy's _Call of Duty_ division. The team, Dallas Empire, competes in the league in the 2020 season.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-25)
Team Envy officially entered the _Counter-Strike_ scene, their first venture into PC Esports, on February 2, 2015, after acquiring the French _Counter-Strike: Global Offensive_ (_CS:GO_) squad of Team LDLC led by captain Vincent "Happy" Schopenhauer.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-26)
texts.8: In March 2015, Envy finished 3rd–4th in their first major appearance, ESL One Katowice 2015, after losing to Ninjas in Pyjamas 0–2 in the semi-finals.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-27) Shortly afterwards, in March, the team won their first ever championship at the Gfinity Spring Masters.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-28) On June 21, 2015, they traded Richard "shox" Papillon and Edouard "SmithZz" Dubourdeaux to Titan in exchange for Kenny "kennyS" Schrub and Dan "apEX" Madesclaire.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-29) With the new roster they finished runners-up at the ESL One Cologne 2015 major, before finally winning their first major championship at DreamHack Open Cluj-Napoca 2015 after defeating Natus Vincere 2–0 in the grand finals.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:8-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:9-31) Following the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks, Envy withdrew from IEM San Jose due to travel safety concerns.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-32) The team ended the 2015 season securing 7 championships and 11 grand final appearances.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33)
texts.9:
In March 2016, following an 11–12th-place finish at IEM Katowice 2016, Envy benched Fabien "kioShiMa" Fiey due to communication problems and LDLC White's Timothée "DEVIL" Démolon replaced him in the starting line-up.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33) However, the change would prove unsuccessful and in October 2016, DEVIL was released with Christophe "SIXER" Xia replacing him.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-35) On January 15, 2017, the team won WESG 2016, securing US$800,000 as part of the largest CS:GO prize pool.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:10-36)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:4-17)
In February 2017, kennyS, apEX, and Nathan "NBK" Schmitt departed to G2 Esports, with Adil "ScreaM" Benrlitom, Cédric "RpK" Guipouy, and Alexandre "xms" Forté joining in their stead.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-38) In late April, Envy officially revealed their academy project.
texts.10:
On June 20, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the _Counter-Strike_ esports scene following the release of their entire CS:GO roster.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-40) On September 27, 2018, they announced a new North American team, signing the core of ex-Splyce.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:15-41) Team Envy disbanded their _CS:GO_ division on January 11, 2021.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-42)
On September 29, 2026, Envy would return to _Counter-Strike_ for their first _Counter-Strike 2_ roster, signing the 3DMAX roster following the French organization's financial troubles.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-43)

texts.11:
The Team Envy _Gears of War_ (_GoW_) division was founded on January 4, 2012, when the organization formed the professional _GoW_ team "EnVyUs MbN".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-44) The team competed in Gears of War 3, where they placed 4th in the LAN tournament Hypefestation 2.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-46)
In October 2015, Envy announced they were re-entering the _GoW_ competitive scene for Gears of War: Ultimate Edition and were revealed as one of eight teams in ESL's GoW Pro League.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-48) In Season 1 of the league, Envy finished runners-up to Denial Esports.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-49) In Season 2, they became champions after defeating Denial in a rematch of the finals following a 12–2 regular season record; the tournament win marked their first ever Gears of War title.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-50) In July 2016, without dropping a single map, Envy won their second title at the Gears eSports European Open in London.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-51)
texts.12:
Heading into _Gears of War 4_, Envy competed in the Coalition's $1 million Gears Pro Circuit.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-52) Their campaign included multiple second-place finishes, as well as the team's third championship in January 2017, when the team dethroned OpTic Gaming at the Mexico City Open, the first ever GoW event in Latin America.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-54)
On June 13, 2017, shortly after the end of the Gears Pro Circuit, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Gears of War esports scene following the transfer of their roster to Echo Fox.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-55)
The Team Envy _Halo_ division was founded on November 10, 2015, when the organization signed a professional esports team for _Halo 5: Guardians_; the roster included Justin "Pistola" Deese and Austin "Mickwen" McCleary.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-57) The team failed to qualify for the 2016 Halo World Championship after being knocked out of the group stages at the NA Regional Finals.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-58)
texts.13:
Their first major breakthrough came in July 2016, when the team finished 3rd place at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Summer Finals.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-59) In the offseason to follow, Envy acquired rookie Cuyler "Huke" Garland and veteran Eric "Snip3down" Wrona.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-60) In November, they obtained their first Halo championship after winning HCS Las Vegas 2016.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:12-61) Shortly afterwards, in December, the team dethroned OpTic Gaming and won their second championship at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Fall Finals.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-62) Their 2016–17 season campaign ended with a runners-up finish at the 2017 Halo World Championship, where the team produced a 5–0 loser's bracket run before losing to OpTic Gaming in the grand finals.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:13-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-64)
In May 2017, Envy won their third Halo championship at HCS Daytona 2017.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-65) Their 2017–18 season campaign ended in April 2018, following a 3rd-place finish at the 2018 Halo World Championship.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:14-66) On May 24, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Halo esports scene following the release of their roster.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-67)
texts.14:
Team Envy announced their return to the _Halo_ esports scene on October 12, 2020, announcing four new players to compete under head coach Alex "Swift Kill" Ramirez for the upcoming _Halo_ franchise game _Halo Infinite_.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-68) After the merger of Envy Gaming and OpTic Gaming in 2021, OpTic took over Team Envy's _Halo_ division.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-69)
On May 18, 2016, after passing Riot's vetting process, Team Envy officially purchased Renegades’ NA LCS spot in a deal reportedly valued in excess of $1 million.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:622-70)
In their inaugural split, following a perfect 4–0 start, Envy finished in 6th place achieving a playoffs berth, where they were eliminated in the first round.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-71) In the last chance Regional Qualifier for the 2016 League of Legends World Championship, the team once again fell short after losing in the second round to eventual winners Cloud9.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-72)
Following the 2017 Spring Split, Envy faced relegation and had to compete in the Summer Promotion Tournament. In the Promotion Tournament, they qualified into the 2017 NA LCS Summer Split after defeating Gold Coin United 3–2 in the loser's bracket finals.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-73)
On November 20, 2017, Team Envy withdrew from League of Legends after their franchise application for the 2018 NA LCS season was declined.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-75)

**Envy** (stylized in all caps as **ENVY**), formerly **Team Envy**, is an American esports franchise based in Dallas, Texas. Founded in 2007 as a professional _Call of Duty_ team under the moniker **Team EnVyUs**, they fielded rosters in _Counter-Strike, FIFA, Fortnite, Gears of War, Halo, League of Legends, Chess, Magic: the Gathering, Overwatch, Paladins, [PUBG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayerUnknown's\_Battlegrounds "PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds"), Rocket League, SMITE, StarCraft, [Super Smash Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros. "Super Smash Bros."), Street Fighter_ and _Valorant_ in their original form. Following the merger between Envy Gaming and OpTic Gaming, Envy Gaming retired the Team Envy brand in June 2022, shifting all of them to the OpTic Gaming moniker.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-2)
On January 17, 2025, Mike "Hastr0" Rufail announced that he had re-acquired the Team Envy name, as well as associated trademarks, from OpTic, reviving the franchise as ENVY.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-EnvyRevival-3) Envy has since entered _Apex Legends_, _Marvel Rivals_, _The Finals_ and _[Rainbow Six Siege X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom\_Clancy's\_Rainbow\_Six\_Siege "Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege")_, as well as re-entering _Counter-Strike_, _Halo_, _Super Smash Bros._ and Valorant (currently as members of the Valorant Champions Tour (VCT) Americas).
Owner and CEO Mike "Hastr0" Rufail played for the team's _Call of Duty_ team.

In July 2017, the team finished runners-up at Stage 2 of the 2017 CWL Global Pro League.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-19) In August 2017, they competed in the 2017 Call of Duty World League Championship where they attempted to become the first back-to-back champions. In the winner's bracket semi-finals they defeated eUnited 3–1, which included their famous second half 0–10 to 12–10 Uplink comeback.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-20) In the winner's bracket final they defeated OpTic to book their place in a record 4th Call of Duty Championship grand finals, however this time around the roster would be heartbroken as they lost both best-of-5 series to OpTic in a rematch to finish in 2nd place.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:7-21)
Heading into _Call of Duty: WWII_, Envy released JKap, Apathy, and John.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-22) In November 2017, they revealed their new roster which included Cuyler "Huke" Garland who had been competing in Team Envy's Halo division as he was too young (under the age of 18) to compete in the Call of Duty World League.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-23)

On September 22, 2018, Envy acquired the roster of Evil Geniuses consisting of ACHES, Apathy, Assault and SiLLy. They will join the organization and pair with Huke to complete the roster.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-24)
Team Envy's parent company Envy Gaming purchased a Call of Duty League slot in late 2019, ending Team Envy's _Call of Duty_ division. The team, Dallas Empire, competes in the league in the 2020 season.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-25)
Team Envy officially entered the _Counter-Strike_ scene, their first venture into PC Esports, on February 2, 2015, after acquiring the French _Counter-Strike: Global Offensive_ (_CS:GO_) squad of Team LDLC led by captain Vincent "Happy" Schopenhauer.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-26)

In March 2015, Envy finished 3rd–4th in their first major appearance, ESL One Katowice 2015, after losing to Ninjas in Pyjamas 0–2 in the semi-finals.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-27) Shortly afterwards, in March, the team won their first ever championship at the Gfinity Spring Masters.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-28) On June 21, 2015, they traded Richard "shox" Papillon and Edouard "SmithZz" Dubourdeaux to Titan in exchange for Kenny "kennyS" Schrub and Dan "apEX" Madesclaire.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-29) With the new roster they finished runners-up at the ESL One Cologne 2015 major, before finally winning their first major championship at DreamHack Open Cluj-Napoca 2015 after defeating Natus Vincere 2–0 in the grand finals.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:8-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:9-31) Following the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks, Envy withdrew from IEM San Jose due to travel safety concerns.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-32) The team ended the 2015 season securing 7 championships and 11 grand final appearances.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33)

In March 2016, following an 11–12th-place finish at IEM Katowice 2016, Envy benched Fabien "kioShiMa" Fiey due to communication problems and LDLC White's Timothée "DEVIL" Démolon replaced him in the starting line-up.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:0-33) However, the change would prove unsuccessful and in October 2016, DEVIL was released with Christophe "SIXER" Xia replacing him.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-35) On January 15, 2017, the team won WESG 2016, securing US$800,000 as part of the largest CS:GO prize pool.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:10-36)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:4-17)
In February 2017, kennyS, apEX, and Nathan "NBK" Schmitt departed to G2 Esports, with Adil "ScreaM" Benrlitom, Cédric "RpK" Guipouy, and Alexandre "xms" Forté joining in their stead.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-38) In late April, Envy officially revealed their academy project.

On June 20, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the _Counter-Strike_ esports scene following the release of their entire CS:GO roster.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-40) On September 27, 2018, they announced a new North American team, signing the core of ex-Splyce.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:15-41) Team Envy disbanded their _CS:GO_ division on January 11, 2021.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-42)
On September 29, 2026, Envy would return to _Counter-Strike_ for their first _Counter-Strike 2_ roster, signing the 3DMAX roster following the French organization's financial troubles.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-43)

The Team Envy _Gears of War_ (_GoW_) division was founded on January 4, 2012, when the organization formed the professional _GoW_ team "EnVyUs MbN".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-44) The team competed in Gears of War 3, where they placed 4th in the LAN tournament Hypefestation 2.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-46)
In October 2015, Envy announced they were re-entering the _GoW_ competitive scene for Gears of War: Ultimate Edition and were revealed as one of eight teams in ESL's GoW Pro League.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-48) In Season 1 of the league, Envy finished runners-up to Denial Esports.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-49) In Season 2, they became champions after defeating Denial in a rematch of the finals following a 12–2 regular season record; the tournament win marked their first ever Gears of War title.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-50) In July 2016, without dropping a single map, Envy won their second title at the Gears eSports European Open in London.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-51)

Heading into _Gears of War 4_, Envy competed in the Coalition's $1 million Gears Pro Circuit.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-52) Their campaign included multiple second-place finishes, as well as the team's third championship in January 2017, when the team dethroned OpTic Gaming at the Mexico City Open, the first ever GoW event in Latin America.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-54)
On June 13, 2017, shortly after the end of the Gears Pro Circuit, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Gears of War esports scene following the transfer of their roster to Echo Fox.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-55)
The Team Envy _Halo_ division was founded on November 10, 2015, when the organization signed a professional esports team for _Halo 5: Guardians_; the roster included Justin "Pistola" Deese and Austin "Mickwen" McCleary.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-57) The team failed to qualify for the 2016 Halo World Championship after being knocked out of the group stages at the NA Regional Finals.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-58)

Their first major breakthrough came in July 2016, when the team finished 3rd place at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Summer Finals.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-59) In the offseason to follow, Envy acquired rookie Cuyler "Huke" Garland and veteran Eric "Snip3down" Wrona.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-60) In November, they obtained their first Halo championship after winning HCS Las Vegas 2016.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:12-61) Shortly afterwards, in December, the team dethroned OpTic Gaming and won their second championship at the NA HCS Pro League - 2016 Fall Finals.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-62) Their 2016–17 season campaign ended with a runners-up finish at the 2017 Halo World Championship, where the team produced a 5–0 loser's bracket run before losing to OpTic Gaming in the grand finals.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:13-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-64)
In May 2017, Envy won their third Halo championship at HCS Daytona 2017.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-65) Their 2017–18 season campaign ended in April 2018, following a 3rd-place finish at the 2018 Halo World Championship.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:14-66) On May 24, 2018, Team Envy announced they had departed from the Halo esports scene following the release of their roster.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-67)

Team Envy announced their return to the _Halo_ esports scene on October 12, 2020, announcing four new players to compete under head coach Alex "Swift Kill" Ramirez for the upcoming _Halo_ franchise game _Halo Infinite_.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-68) After the merger of Envy Gaming and OpTic Gaming in 2021, OpTic took over Team Envy's _Halo_ division.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-69)
On May 18, 2016, after passing Riot's vetting process, Team Envy officially purchased Renegades’ NA LCS spot in a deal reportedly valued in excess of $1 million.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-:622-70)
In their inaugural split, following a perfect 4–0 start, Envy finished in 6th place achieving a playoffs berth, where they were eliminated in the first round.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-71) In the last chance Regional Qualifier for the 2016 League of Legends World Championship, the team once again fell short after losing in the second round to eventual winners Cloud9.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-72)
Following the 2017 Spring Split, Envy faced relegation and had to compete in the Summer Promotion Tournament. In the Promotion Tournament, they qualified into the 2017 NA LCS Summer Split after defeating Gold Coin United 3–2 in the loser's bracket finals.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-73)
On November 20, 2017, Team Envy withdrew from League of Legends after their franchise application for the 2018 NA LCS season was declined.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy_(esports)#cite_note-75)

# Dennis Quaid, wife Kimberly divorcing ‘with mutual respect’
By Frank Lovece
…Comments
Posted on June 29, 2016
Actor Dennis Quaid and his third wife, Kimberly Buffington Quaid, have announced they are divorcing.
Video 3
Video 4
Skip Ad
“After careful consideration, we have decided to end our 12-year marriage,” the couple said in a statement Wednesday to TMZ.com. “The decision was made amicably and with mutual respect toward one another.”
The two had met in Austin, Texas, in March 2003, when a mutual friend introduced them at a dinner. They married on July 4, 2004, and had twins Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace on Nov. 8, 2007. Quaid, 62, also has a son, actor Jack Quaid, 24, with his second wife, Meg Ryan, to whom he was married from 1991 to 2001. He previously was wed to actress P.J. Soles from 1978 to 1983.
Buffington Quaid initially filed for divorce on March 2, 2012, citing irreconcilable differences, but the couple soon reunited. She then filed for legal separation on Oct. 19 of that year, with Dennis Quaid subsequently filing for divorce that Nov. 30. Though the actor’s representative the following March denied rumors that the couple had reconciled, telling E! News, “They are divorcing,” they withdrew the petition by that September.

# Dennis Quaid, wife Kimberly divorcing ‘with mutual respect’
By Frank Lovece
…Comments
Posted on June 29, 2016
Actor Dennis Quaid and his third wife, Kimberly Buffington Quaid, have announced they are divorcing.
Video 3
Video 4
Skip Ad
“After careful consideration, we have decided to end our 12-year marriage,” the couple said in a statement Wednesday to TMZ.com. “The decision was made amicably and with mutual respect toward one another.”
The two had met in Austin, Texas, in March 2003, when a mutual friend introduced them at a dinner. They married on July 4, 2004, and had twins Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace on Nov. 8, 2007. Quaid, 62, also has a son, actor Jack Quaid, 24, with his second wife, Meg Ryan, to whom he was married from 1991 to 2001. He previously was wed to actress P.J. Soles from 1978 to 1983.
Buffington Quaid initially filed for divorce on March 2, 2012, citing irreconcilable differences, but the couple soon reunited. She then filed for legal separation on Oct. 19 of that year, with Dennis Quaid subsequently filing for divorce that Nov. 30. Though the actor’s representative the following March denied rumors that the couple had reconciled, telling E! News, “They are divorcing,” they withdrew the petition by that September.

1.  **Sports Team Founded:** Between 2010 and 2015 (inclusive).
2.  **Founder:** A specific person who founded the team.
3.  **Previous Company:** This person previously founded a company.
4.  **Company Announcement:** The company announced, in a year between 1998 and 2006 (inclusive), that they would launch a video game in Europe in a year between 2002 and 2008 (inclusive).
5.  **Marriage Rumors:** Between 2005 and 2010 (inclusive), this company publicly denied rumors about the founder's possible marriage.
6.  **Championship:** Between 2012 and 2022 (inclusive), the mentioned sports team won a championship.
7.  **Question:** What is the name of the mentioned sports team?

**Analysis of Clues:**

*   **Clue 5 (Marriage Rumors):** A video game founder denying marriage rumors between 2005-2010 is a very specific identifier. I recall Will Wright co-founded Maxis (EA) but his personal life isn't typically tabloid fodder in that way for *his* own marriage denial as a corporate announcement. Let me check other famous founders.
*   **Clue 4 (Game Launch Europe):** This implies a publisher or developer announcing a release window.
*   **Clue 1 & 6 (Team & Championship):** An esports team founded by a game founder.
*   Let's search for "video game founder denied marriage rumors" again, specifically looking for the person who denies rumors about their *possible* marriage while at their company.

Let's try searching for "video game founder denied marriage rumors 2007".
Wait, earlier search results mentioned "Howard Stern" denying rumors he was leaving... not relevant.
"Dennis Quaid" denied rumors of reconciliation... actor.
"Halle Berry" dating Gabriel Aubry... not founder.

Let's rethink the "denied rumors about possible marriage".
Maybe it's **Peter Molyneux**? He had many rumors. But did he found a team?
Maybe it's **Jens Bergenstrahle** (King)?
Maybe it's **Markus Persson**? No.

Let's go back to the "company announced video game launch in Europe" part.
And the "sports team founded by this person".
Perhaps the person is **Andy Miller**? No, Nadeshot is an esports player turned owner of 100 Thieves (founded 2015). Did 100 Threes win a championship? Yes. But did he found a video game company? He worked for Activision.
Did Activision announce a game launch in Europe between 2002-2008? Yes, many.
Did Activision deny marriage rumors about Andy Miller/Nadeshot? He was born in 1992, so no.

Let's consider **Tomonobu Itagaki**? No.
**David Cage**? No.

What if the person is **Gabe Newell** (Valve)? No marriage rumors there.
What if it's **Sylvain Gohier** (Ubisoft Paris)?

Let's search for "video game founder denied rumors marriage" again with different terms like "tabloids" or "press conference".

Singers Nana Mizuki and T.M. Revolution (Takanori Nishikawa) both denied rumors that had been circulating online that the two of them had gotten married. Nishikawa said regarding the rumors, "They are absolutely not true, so everyone please be at ease." Nishikawa also joked that even his mother was surprised when she heard the rumor. Mizuki also said she was surprised about the rumor.
The two had collaborated to perform the opening theme song "Preserved Roses" for the first season of Valvrave the Liberator, and the two will once again perform the opening theme song for the anime's second season. The CD single for "Preserved Roses" ranked #2 in its first week of sales in May by selling 115,000.
_Source: Nikkan Sports_

Singers Nana Mizuki and T.M. Revolution (Takanori Nishikawa) both denied rumors that had been circulating online that the two of them had gotten married. Nishikawa said regarding the rumors, "They are absolutely not true, so everyone please be at ease." Nishikawa also joked that even his mother was surprised when she heard the rumor. Mizuki also said she was surprised about the rumor.
The two had collaborated to perform the opening theme song "Preserved Roses" for the first season of Valvrave the Liberator, and the two will once again perform the opening theme song for the anime's second season. The CD single for "Preserved Roses" ranked #2 in its first week of sales in May by selling 115,000.
_Source: Nikkan Sports_
